Visual result can only be judged by looking at it.
Cleanup and low power handling are present, which is a good sign.

terms.meaning: a browser feature that lets code draw 3D graphics using the computer's graphics chip.
a picture made of many small dots rather than solid surfaces.
a small program that runs on the graphics chip to decide how each dot looks.
a region's anchor point on the brain, where its label sits.

sections.name: File setup
sections.title: Design notes and imports
sections.what: Brings in the 3D library and the brain data. The header comment records the design: a top-down view, a light blue left hemisphere for logic and work, and a gold right hemisphere for curiosity and craft.
sections.why: Records the intended look so later changes keep it.

sections.name: BrainCallbacks
sections.title: Pick callback shape
sections.what: Defines the one callback the scene uses to report a picked node to the page. It passes a node id or nothing.
sections.why: Keeps the 3D code separate from the page, which only receives picks.

sections.name: ScreenPoint
sections.title: Screen point shape
sections.what: Describes where a node or hub appears on screen and whether it is in front of the camera.
sections.why: Lets page labels sit exactly on the brain.

sections.name: rng, BLUE, GOLD
sections.title: Random generator and colours
sections.what: Provides a repeatable random number generator and the two brand colours, light blue and gold.
sections.why: A repeatable generator keeps the dot cloud identical on each visit.
sections.watch_out: Changing the seed number changes the shape of the whole brain.

sections.name: fold
sections.title: Fold pattern
sections.what: Calculates a value between 0 and 1 for each point, high on ridges and low in grooves, which gives the wrinkled surface.
sections.why: Likely reason: this makes the brain look like folded tissue rather than a smooth ball.
sections.watch_out: Small changes to these numbers change every fold, so check the look by eye after any edit.

sections.name: cortex
sections.title: Hemisphere shape
sections.what: Maps a direction on a sphere to a point on a brain-shaped surface, one hemisphere at a time. It also flattens the underside and the inner side.
sections.why: Gives the rough brain outline that the dots are placed on.
sections.watch_out: Only the upper part is drawn, so the underside is never shown.

sections.name: BrainScene (part 1)
sections.title: Scene setup
sections.what: Creates the renderer, camera, group and window listeners, then builds the cortex and nodes and starts the animation loop.
sections.why: Everything is set up once when the scene is created so the animation can run.
sections.watch_out: Low power mode is decided only at creation, so a later window resize does not change the point count.

sections.name: BrainScene: buildCortex
sections.title: Building the cortex dots
sections.what: Creates about 110,000 dots across both hemispheres, gathered on the ridges, coloured by hemisphere and depth, and drawn with a custom shader that fades distant dots.
sections.why: Gathering dots on ridges makes the folds easier to read.
sections.watch_out: The point count drives most of the cost, so changes here affect speed on every device.

sections.name: BrainScene (part 3)
sections.title: Placing and drawing knowledge nodes
sections.what: Places each knowledge node on the surface near its region's hub, with a small random spread, then builds the node point set with its colour.
sections.why: Keeps related nodes clustered in the same area of the brain.
sections.watch_out: Hub positions depend on the order of regions on each side, so reordering the data moves the hubs.

sections.name: BrainScene (part 4)
sections.title: Node look and highlight refresh
sections.what: Draws each node as a dot that grows and brightens when selected or highlighted. Then it recalculates which nodes and links are shown when focus or region changes.
sections.why: Only the chosen node and its direct links are shown, which keeps the view readable.
sections.watch_out: Links are rebuilt on every focus change, so a very large link set could slow things down.

sections.name: BrainScene: setRegion
sections.title: Region, drag and tap picking
sections.what: Sets the active region and handles dragging to turn the brain, as well as taps to pick. A tap is a press with less than 6 pixels of movement. It picks the nearest visible node within about 22 pixels.
sections.why: Separates a drag from a tap so turning the brain does not pick a node by accident.
sections.watch_out: The 6 pixel and 22 pixel limits set how forgiving taps feel. Changing them changes how easy picking is.

sections.name: BrainScene (part 6)
sections.title: Resize, animation loop and cleanup
sections.what: Fits the camera to the container's shape, then runs a per-frame loop that gently sways the brain unless reduced motion is on or the visitor is dragging. Each frame it also records node screen positions. Dispose stops the loop and frees memory.
sections.why: Recording screen positions every frame keeps page labels in step with the moving brain.
sections.watch_out: Dispose must run when the page unmounts, or the loop and listeners keep running.

summary: Draws the hero brain as a glowing point cloud on a canvas, lets visitors turn it and tap knowledge nodes, and reports where nodes and region hubs appear on screen.
purpose: Provides the 3D knowledge map visual used in the hero area.
why: Likely reason: the brain is drawn in 3D while the readable labels are kept in normal page HTML, so the text stays sharp and the picture stays clean. The code comment says depth comes from size and fading.
how: 1. Builds a dot cortex from two hemisphere shapes with a ridge pattern. 2. Places knowledge nodes near their region hubs. 3. Sets up the renderer, camera and pointer handling. 4. Each frame, rotates the brain, draws it, and records where each node and hub sits on screen. 5. A tap picks the nearest visible node within about 22 pixels. 6. Dispose frees all drawing parts and listeners.
inputs: A container element, a callback for picks, a reduced motion flag, a low power flag, and data from the brain data file (nodes, links and regions).
outputs: A drawn brain on a canvas, screen positions for nodes and hubs read by HeroBrain, and a pick callback with a node id or nothing.
risks: Uses about 110,000 points on normal devices and about 60,000 in low power mode. Several window listeners are added, so dispose must run when the page unmounts or they stay active.
debug: If nothing shows, check WebGL support and the container's size. If taps miss their target, check the screen positions. If the page is slow, check the low power decision and the point count. If the brain looks dark, check the colour values and the fade settings.
